value.overview: The Ruddy Duck is a compact diving duck with a stiff, often upturned tail and a broad bill. Breeding males have a chestnut body, black head, white cheek patch, and bright blue bill. Females and nonbreeding birds are duller brown with a dark cap and pale cheek. It breeds mainly in freshwater marshes and ponds across North and Central America and uses wetlands, lakes, reservoirs, and sheltered coastal waters outside the breeding season.
value.classification: The Ruddy Duck belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the stiff-tailed duck genus Oxyura. It is one of the characteristic stiff-tailed diving ducks of the Americas.
value.identification: This small, thick-necked duck has a short, broad bill, a rounded body, and a long, narrow tail that is frequently held upright. The breeding male is especially distinctive, with a rich reddish-brown body, black crown and face, white cheek, and vivid blue bill. Females, juveniles, and males in eclipse plumage are gray-brown, with a dark cap, pale cheek, and softly streaked body. It dives readily and often sits low in the water.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Duck is native from western and central North America south through Mexico and parts of Central America, with additional resident populations in the Caribbean and northern South America. It favors freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, ponds, reservoirs, and wetlands with dense emergent vegetation. In Costa Rica it is a rare, localized visitor rather than a common resident; records are associated with suitable inland wetlands and lakes, and there is no well-established breeding population documented for the country.
value.migrationStatus: Most northern populations migrate south in small flocks, often at night, for winter. In Costa Rica, the species is best treated as an uncommon to rare migrant or winter visitor, with occasional records rather than regular widespread occurrence. Some populations farther south and in the Caribbean are resident.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs in freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, ponds, and prairie wetlands bordered by dense aquatic vegetation. The nest is a concealed, floating or supported structure made from marsh plants. Females may lay eggs in the nests of other waterfowl, a behavior known as nest parasitism. Clutches commonly contain several large, pale eggs. Males perform conspicuous displays involving head movements, body postures, and vocal or mechanical sounds, while females provide most parental care.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Duck feeds by diving and by picking food from the water surface or vegetation. Its diet includes aquatic plants, seeds, algae, pondweeds, sedges, and grasses, along with aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, and other small invertebrates. Animal food is often particularly important during the breeding season, while plant material may form a larger part of the diet at other times.
value.behavior: Ruddy Ducks are strong divers and spend much of their time on open water, where they may forage, rest, or escape danger by submerging. They are usually quiet and unobtrusive outside the breeding season. Birds may gather in loose flocks, especially during migration and winter. When alarmed, they often dive rather than fly immediately. Their pointed tails and low swimming posture are useful field marks, and migration commonly takes place at night.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered threatened, although abundance varies among regions and local wetland populations may fluctuate.
